questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to study politics from a more comparative perspective - i.e. how migration is managed in the UK compared to other European countries. Furthermore, I wished to study more closely the political, sociological and economic drivers behind the UK's relationship with the EU. At Queen Mary I had the opportunity to do so.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I really recommend going abroad for just a term or two. It has been a great experience both academically and personally

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: I think it was quite easy. The information letters/email from the Study Abroad services at the University of Copenhagen and Queen Mary provided the essential information I needed. As a student you must read these emails as a manual - following every step.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: The information letters/email from the Study Abroad services at Queen Mary provided the essential information I needed. As a student you must read these emails as a manual - following every step. Once every two week, I received a mail describing how to enroll, select courses, what to do in the area, how write an academic assignment in the UK educational system etc.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: It was very good. I am very satisfied. The "study abroad team" answered all my questions quickly and kindly. The orientation in the first week was thorough assisting students academically and in relation to our general well-being. They were aware of the transition needed in order to live and study in a new country.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: It was quite easy. A friend of mine recommended "KFUK i London". They own 6 appartements in London and they prioritise letting out the appartements to Danish students. My girlfriend and I applied and got one of the appartments.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
If you are renting an apartment then you might need to pay "Council Tax". Ask your Landlord in advance. Most students can be exempted from paying the tax. I found the process of applying for exemption quite sluggish - so patience is a good thing. 

It is easy to get around in London so you should not be afraid if you find yourself living off campus

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The information letters from the host institution were very informative.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: Before arriving the host institution have a "pre-registration periode". In this periode you apply for the classes you want to take. After the two-week registration periode, the responsible academic department then decides whether or not you get the class. In the first two-weeks of the term you can then apply for changes to your courses - and many students attend one lecture in the first weeks in order to figure out whether they like the course. After the two first weeks of term the registration to classes are final.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The study abroad team was very helpfull - both in person and writing (mail).

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: In the pre-registration periode both of my desired classes was approved. But just before the first lecture, one of my classes was canceled. I then used the first week of the term to find another class. I found one I liked, applied and got registered successfully.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Take your time when readying the informative emails from the host institution - and do not be afraid to reach out and ask the administration questions. I have been writing to both lectures, study abroad officers and administrative personal and they have all been keen to help me.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: As in Denmark, you do not have much in-class teachings. The amount of academic content you receive is heavily dependent on your own effort in reading the required readings. I did not find the amount of reading overwhelming but the lectures provided a long list of optional reading every week - so the workload can be heavy if you choose it to be.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The courses I could take was on the highest level available at the masters programme of Queen Mary. In general the academic level of the lectures was equivalent to that of a "elective course" at my home university. Some of the required readings was less heavy and more factual (e.g. reports from NGO's and podcasts) than I have been used to at home. So I think an average Danish exchange student would find the level comfortable and not too challenging.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: It was very much alike. The weekly two-hour classes consisted of approximately one hour lecture followed by an hour of student-led seminars with either presentations or discussions in groups.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
1) International Migration and Public Policy 
2) From Blitz to Brexit: Britain and the EU

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I can recommend both. I would especially recommend the course "From Blitz to Brexit: Britain and the EU" if you are interested in British Politics and Brexit. The course is structured chronologically, so every week you study the UK-EU relationship from a new decade under a new Prime Minister. You get an in-depth understanding of UK's European politics during Wilson, Thatcher, Major, Blair, Brown, Cameron, and others.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Council Tax if you do not get an exemption. I also needed to pay for a language course before enrolling.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: If you use the tube then transportation is more expensive than expected. The bus is less expensive than expected. Food prices are roughly the same as in Denmark.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I was positively surprised by the amount of activities. There are many student organisations and a very well-run student union. They host pub quiz, football games, have a local pub, trips to the cinema, walking tours and more. More activities are supplied than you will be able to attend.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: All kinds of sport (badminton, football, running, swimming etc.), creative classes, bingo, pub quiz, guided tours in the neighbourhood, museum tours etc. There a plenty of opportunities.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Going with the locals on pubs. You need not to drink alcohol - but attending pub quiz or watching a football match is fun at a pub.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Try to walk around in different neighbourhoods (Shoreditch, Sloane Square, Hampstead, Richmond). Every place has its own style and vibe. London is much more than the West End (Big Ben, Westminister and Soho). Even though London is not a cheap city - you can visit lots of places on a tight budget by taking the buses, walking and visiting free parks and museums.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: London is a multicultural city. You will probably meet as many foreigners as Brits in London so the "local" culture is not as visible in the city. In general people are nice, polite and used to foreigners like yourself.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Attend the social events on campus and do not be shy to ask the British students about British culture. Ask them about Sunday Roast and say you enjoy British food (then you will get friends).

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Generally no challenging cultural differences.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The humour. It is sarcastic and very much like the Danish humour. I also appreciate the fact that you can communicate with everyone (unlike other places in Europe where language is a barrier).

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Reach out to the Study Abroad Team at the host university if you have any questions - they are kind. 
2. Take a course where you learn something about Britain  
3. Take the buses to get around

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: No

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Meeting local students and other associate students. I found it very rewarding to talk with other students with a different academic background than my own. It brings a new dynamic to studying.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Getting wifi and Council Tax exemption. You might need to get a British bank account in order to do so.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
